abstract: |
  A scientific study passes through many hands, each working with a different artifact. The study moves from the researcher to the ethics committee and the participant, then on to the software engineer, the analyst, the reviewer, and the replicator. The artifact changes at each step: a protocol PDF and an experiment script become a dataset and a preprocessing notebook, then a manuscript figure and a CONSORT diagram. Because these artifacts drift apart, no single representation describes the study as it was actually run. Cognitive science has standardized the data; the process that produces the data is still left to prose and code. We set out the requirements that a specification language must meet to close this gap, and we present *Studyflow*, a framework that meets them. At its core a study is a typed directed graph, implemented as an extension of Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) with elements specific to experimental cognitive science: domain-specific activities (cognitive task, questionnaire, instruction), decision gateways (randomization, eligibility), data operations (map, filter, reduce), and data elements bound to community standards (BIDS, Psych-DS, CSVW). A single Studyflow file is at once the protocol, the specification, the publication figure, and the participant-facing application. We describe the language, an open-source modeler, and a runner, projected into multiple views of one source tailored for difference audience. To demonstrate the framework end to end, we follow one study from protocol design to publication. The same file enrolls human participants and a cohort of artificial agents, including RL agents, cognitive models, and language models in one randomized controlled trial. Human and agent responses shows where they agree across tasks and where they diverge.
impact-statement: |
  The diagram an ethics board approves becomes the app participants run, the pipeline that analyzes their data, and the figure in the published paper. Studyflow makes a study's process a single source of truth that can be reviewed, executed, and published, in place of the divergent artifacts (protocols, checklists, scripts, pipeline parameters, figures) that fragment experimental research today.

# 1. Introduction

## 1.1 The reproducibility gap is in *processes*, not just data

A scientific study touches many people and systems. A researcher designs it; an ethics committee approves it; a participant runs it; a data pipeline ingests it; a model trains on it; a reviewer reads it as a manuscript; and a replicator tries to rebuild it. Reproducing the study later requires more than the data and the manuscript. It also requires an explicit and complete description of the *processes* that generated them [@aguilar2022experiments; @momeni2026guidelines]. A complete description of any computing system needs both a data model (for its structure) and a process model (for its behavior) [@olive2007conceptual]. In cognitive sciences, however, most standardization has focused on the data, so the processes that produce the data are documented only in narrative prose, ad-hoc lab conventions, box-and-arrow diagrams, or code repositories that drift away from the text they accompany [@bell2021perspectives; @osc2015]. The community has built strong standards for the data plane, notably BIDS and Psych-DS; the process plane, a machine-readable record of how those data came to be, has no equivalent. That asymmetry, not a shortage of data standards, is the gap this paper addresses.

The cost of this missing process model becomes clear whenever someone other than the author has to re-read a study. It is largest in neuroscience and clinical research, where one study may record EEG, fMRI, eye tracking, and behavior at once, pass through an ethics board and a trial registry, and end in a CONSORT flow diagram, each modality and each stage adding an artifact that must stay consistent with the rest. The researcher's protocol PDF, the ethics application, the experiment script, the preprocessing notebook, the model card, the manuscript figure, and the CONSORT diagram all begin as different views of the same study, and they end as inconsistent ones. By that point, no single artifact describes the study *as it was actually run*. Reviewers and replicators reach the code and data through these artifacts, so divergence among them limits how far the code and data can be independently checked. Trust in research is built or lost at this point of divergence.

The usual way to compensate for a missing process model is voluntary narrative reporting: checklists, pre-registration forms, and journal endorsements. The available evidence suggests it has limited effect. A cross-sectional study of 400 psychology articles published in 2022 found that 7% to 14% had been preregistered and 14% to 16% shared raw data, despite more than a decade of reform [@hardwicke2024prevalence], and gaps between endorsement and adherence recur across fields and journal policies [@percie2020arrive; @hair2019iicarus; @hardwicke2024transparency]. The reason is structural rather than a matter of researcher compliance. A checklist records *what to mention* without requiring *what to share*, and it accepts a narrative description of a process in place of a formal, verifiable one, so the underlying process model stays implicit and open to interpretation.

We argue that reproducibility should be a property of the shared artifact itself, rather than separate documentation kept alongside the work. A single representation of a study that is machine-readable, human-understandable, and shared across its many audiences would keep the process model and the data model aligned. The contribution of this paper is one concrete version of that idea, built on a standard process notation and a working open-source tool that others can replace without losing the underlying specification.

## 1.2 Current practice fragments the study across artifacts

Today, each audience of a study tends to work from a different artifact, and these artifacts are difficult to keep consistent with one another. We group current approaches into a few overlapping families.

- *Box-and-arrow figures* in manuscripts communicate study logic at a glance, but they are not standardized, not machine-verifiable, and rarely connected to the code that runs the study. Each one is tailored to a particular stakeholder: a CONSORT flow for a journal, a slide deck for a funding agency, or a sketch on a whiteboard for an engineer [@bogale2024].
- *Checklists and pre-registration forms* are cataloged through the EQUATOR network [@simera2010equator] and provide structured text. They store it, however, in free-form fields and in binary or proprietary formats such as PDF or DOCX, in data silos that are difficult to place under version control.
- *Data standards, ontologies, and packages*, including BIDS, Psych-DS, and CSVW [@bids; @psychds; @csvw], make the data machine-readable, but they say little about the processes that produced it. Ontology-based process models are numerous, but they require high upfront effort and are rarely reused [@norouzi2025semantic_processes].
- *Code and configuration*, from analysis scripts, GitHub Actions, and Nextflow [@kinsman2021] to registries such as protocols.io [@teytelman2016], make pipelines precise. They require domain-specific programming skills, however, that are not accessible to ethics boards, reviewers, and many collaborators.

The recurring pattern is a split between *execution* and *communication*. Tools that execute the study, such as scripts, workflow engines, and CI pipelines, are aimed at developers and machines, while tools that communicate it, such as protocol PDFs, narrative platforms, and reporting checklists, are aimed at humans. Even provenance systems, which track the computational graph well, rarely capture the full experimental context of eligibility decisions, randomization, manual annotations, and protocol deviations, leaving a boundary between a well-tracked computational graph and a partially represented experimental one [@souza2020provenance; @simmons2018provenance_sport]. No single representation spans the full lifecycle of a study in a form that scientists, engineers, funding agencies, ethics boards, and journal editors can all read, validate, and execute (Figure 1).

## 1.3 BPMN as a foundation

Building this single representation is a language-design problem. Experimental cognitive science meets the standard criteria for a domain-specific modeling language: recurring structural patterns across studies, expert users who would benefit from a familiar notation rather than general-purpose code, and no executable language that already covers the whole experiment lifecycle [@mernik2005dsl]. Rather than invent a new graphical language, we extend an established one whose visual conventions are already used elsewhere, because a notation that researchers, engineers, and reviewers already recognize is a cheaper starting point, and the principles that make a visual notation effective are themselves a research topic [@moody2009physics].

Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) is a mature, ISO-standard graphical language for processes [@white2004introduction]. It already provides what scientific workflows need (events, activities, sub-processes, gateways, data objects, sequence and data flows, and choreography between participants), an established tooling ecosystem (editors such as `bpmn-js` and Camunda Modeler, and drawing libraries such as diagrams.net), and a standard serialization, BPMN 2.0 XML, that engineers and analysts already recognize and that outlives any single tool.

We build on two of BPMN's extension mechanisms: `extensionElements` and namespaced attributes. The standard lets authors add domain-specific elements and attributes inside a new namespace, so a BPMN-only parser ignores them gracefully while a domain-aware tool can validate and render them [@magnani2009bpdmn]. Domain-specific profiles already follow this pattern across clinical pathways [@braun2014], serverless machine-learning pipelines [@tetzlaff2022bpmn4sml], human-AI collaboration [@ait2024bpmn_humanagent], and healthcare [@pufahl2022], with dozens more cataloged and classified against the BPMN core [@zarour2019; @braun2014classification]. Cognitive and behavioral research is missing from this list.

<!--
Recent large-language-model-assisted BPMN authoring tools (ProMoAI, BPMN-ChatBot, and related work [@kourani2024promoai; @kourani2024process_modeling_llm]) accelerate diagram authoring from text, but evaluations show that competitive syntactic quality does not translate into domain-specific semantics or domain-specific validation [@lauer2026assessing]. Authoring help is welcome; it is not a substitute for a profile that defines what *cognitive task*, *random assignment*, or *eligibility check* mean inside a process model. That profile is the gap Studyflow fills. -->

## 1.4 Design requirements for a study specification language

A specification that closes the process-model gap (§1.1) must meet several requirements at once.

1. **Single source of truth.** One artifact must serve at once as the protocol, the runnable study, the analysis pipeline, and the publication figure, so that the views cannot drift apart.

2. **Executable rather than merely descriptive.** The specification must run, so that a runner walks the same file a reviewer reads.

3. **Legible to every audience without code.** Scientists, ethics boards, reviewers, and engineers must be able to read one diagram rather than four documents in four formats.

4. **Grounded in standards and gracefully degrading.** The specification must be valid BPMN 2.0 that opens in any compliant tool, with bindings to community data standards such as BIDS, Psych-DS, CSVW, and BDM, and its domain extensions must degrade gracefully in a generic tool.

5. **Process and data on one canvas.** Control flow and typed, schema-bound data must live in the same artifact, joined by data associations.

6. **Extensible without forking.** New domain semantics must plug in as optional layers over a tool-independent schema, so that adding a cognitive or acquisition vocabulary does not change the core.

7. **Executor-agnostic.** Who executes the protocol, a person or an artificial agent, must be a runtime choice rather than a property of the diagram, so that one topology enrolls human and agent co-subjects into one schema-conformant table.

The rest of the paper is organized around these requirements: the framework (§2.1 through §2.4) is presented as meeting them, the worked study (§3.1 through §3.5) exercises them, and the discussion (§4) revisits where they hold and where they do not.

## 1.5 Contributions

Studyflow delivers on R1 through R7 as five artifacts, each usable on its own:

1. **A versioned language specification** for Studyflow, written as a LinkML schema [@moxon2025linkml] that serves as the single source of truth for element types, attribute constraints, and validation rules, with FAIR-aligned [@fair] serialization. The schema does not depend on any particular implementation, so a third party can target it directly without relying on the modeler's code.

2. **A layered set of runtime schemas** that mirror the LinkML specification in the YAML format that BPMN tooling reads. They consist of the language core, a companion cognitive layer, and four optional domain extensions: a cognitive-assessment battery, a generic process orchestration layer, a large-scale data transformation layer, and a multimodal acquisition layer for EEG and eye tracking. New domain semantics plug in without changing the core.

3. **A library of worked example diagrams** that ship with the modeler, including a complete CONSORT 2025 randomized-trial template, a SPIRIT 2025 protocol schedule, and patterns for cognitive tasks, data collection, analysis pipelines, MLOps, multi-agent choreography, and reporting guidelines.

4. **The Studyflow Modeler**, an open-source client-side web application (MIT-licensed) for authoring, inspecting, simulating, validating, and publishing Studyflow diagrams. Its inspector and palette are generated from the schemas, so the language and the editor stay in sync.

5. **The Studyflow Runner**, a separate client-side application that parses, validates, and walks a Studyflow file step by step. It ships with built-in renderers for consents, instructions, questionnaire instruments (PHQ-9, GAD-7, BDI-II), generic tasks, and cognitive-assessment tasks; it supports seeded determinism for reproducible random branches; and it drives human participants, classic reinforcement-learning agents, recurrent cognitive models, and language-model agents from the same diagram, each addressed as an actor behind one message-passing executor interface.

# 2. The Studyflow framework

This section presents the Studyflow framework, the paper's primary contribution: a language (§2.1), a modeler (§2.2), a runner (§2.3), and four views of one source (§2.4). Together these artifacts are designed to satisfy the requirements R1-R7 set out in §1.4. A single `.studyflow` source feeds all three artifacts and renders in four ways (Study, Gantt, Checklist, Figure) for different readers, so the same file is at once the protocol, the runnable study, the analysis, and the publication figure.

Each requirement is met by a specific part of the framework, summarized in @tbl-requirements and developed in the subsections that follow.

::: {#tbl-requirements .list-table header-rows=1 aligns="l,l" tbl-colwidths="[42,58]"}
The seven design requirements of §1.4 and where the framework meets each.

- - Requirement (§1.4)
  - Where the framework meets it

- - R1 Single source of truth
  - One shared `.studyflow` source is at once the protocol, the runnable study, the analysis, and the figure (§2.1-§2.4)

- - R2 Executable, not merely descriptive
  - The runner walks the same file a reviewer reads (§2.3)

- - R3 Legible to every audience without code
  - Four reader-facing views project from one source (§2.4)

- - R4 Grounded in standards, gracefully degrading
  - A valid BPMN 2.0 host with bindings to BIDS, Psych-DS, CSVW, and BDM (§2.1)

- - R5 Process and data on one canvas
  - Typed, schema-bound data joined to control flow by data associations (§2.1)

- - R6 Extensible without forking
  - A layered, tool-independent LinkML schema (§2.1-§2.2)

- - R7 Executor-agnostic
  - One executor interface behind the runner, demonstrated end to end in §3.2 (§2.3)
:::

To show that the framework meets R1-R7 in practice rather than in principle, the paper then walks a single study end to end through it, from protocol to publication (§3). That demonstration is subordinate to the framework: it is an existence proof that the capability holds, and the empirical numbers it reports about human and artificial actors are illustrative of what the framework enables rather than a finding about agents in their own right.

## 2.1 Studyflow as a formal object

A Studyflow is a typed, attributed directed graph, a tuple $(N, E, T, \tau, \lambda)$, where $N$ is a finite set of nodes (events, activities, and gateways), $E \subseteq N \times N$ is a set of directed edges (sequence flows and data associations), $T$ is the set of node types the language defines, $\tau: N \to T$ assigns a type to each node, and $\lambda$ attaches typed attributes to each node, such as the `instrument` of a cognitive task, the `probabilityFunction` of a random gateway, or the `onset` and `duration` that drive the Gantt view. The type set $T$ and the attributes admissible on each type are fixed by a versioned schema (below), and a diagram is well-formed exactly when its nodes, edges, and attributes validate against that schema. The graph is general rather than acyclic. Boundary events, message flows, and choreography express the interrupts, loops, and multi-party exchanges that experimental procedures contain, which a directed acyclic graph can represent only through external control logic. Everything that follows in this section is grounded in this one object, and the four reader-facing views of §2.4 are projections of it.

**A standard host notation.** Studyflow realizes this abstract object as a domain-specific profile of Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) 2.0 [@white2004introduction], tailored to experimental research in cognitive sciences. We host the object in BPMN, instead of inventing a new language, for three reasons. First, Studyflow diagrams stay valid BPMN 2.0 XML and open in any compliant tool (Camunda Modeler, bpmn.io, and diagrams.net). Second, BPMN's flowchart-like visual grammar is already familiar to many researchers, which lowers the barrier to adoption; readers new to flowcharts still face a learning curve, but a gentler one than a custom language would impose. Third, BPMN provides a formal extension mechanism (`extensionElements`, namespaced attributes) that adds the domain semantics of $T$ and $\lambda$ without breaking the base standard [@stroppi2011; @magnani2009bpdmn].

**What Studyflow inherits.** Studyflow reuses BPMN's full vocabulary for control flow and structure: start, end, intermediate, boundary, timer, and error *events*; tasks, sub-processes, and call activities; exclusive, parallel, inclusive, event-based, and complex *gateways*; sequence flows and message flows; data objects and data stores with their associations; pools and lanes; and choreography for multi-agent interactions. These elements use standard BPMN shapes and behave as the OMG specifies.

**What Studyflow adds.** Four areas extend BPMN with vocabulary that experimental research routinely needs. First, a top-level **study container** groups every other element and carries study-level metadata (title, version, authors, runtime). Second, **domain-specific activity types** specialize the generic BPMN task with research-meaningful kinds (cognitive tasks, questionnaires, instructions, rest periods, video games, and a curated cognitive battery); each one shows a distinctive icon but remains a normal BPMN task underneath. Third, **research-specific data elements** add bindings to community schemas (BIDS [@bids], Psych-DS [@psychds], CSVW) and to our own Behaverse Data Model (BDM) [@bdm], on top of BPMN's generic data objects, and a small **data-operations vocabulary** (map, filter, reduce, group, transform, and compose) shows the *kind* of transformation as a task marker, so the flow of data is visible at a glance. Fourth, **research gateways** encode the branching patterns specific to experimental design: a random gateway for randomization, a stratified-allocation gateway, and an eligibility gateway that lists inclusion and exclusion criteria. Optional temporal attributes (onset, duration, progress) attach to activities and events, so the Gantt view can derive trial schedules and visit calendars from the same diagram.

**What Studyflow deliberately leaves alone.** Studyflow does not redefine BPMN's serialization conventions, and it leaves XML namespaces, element identifiers, and the base shape vocabulary untouched. Domain extensions live inside BPMN's native extension slot, so a generic BPMN renderer ignores them gracefully while a Studyflow-aware tool validates and renders them consistently.

**A layered set of schemas.** The vocabulary is split into a small core and optional domain extensions that load on demand (Figure 2). The core covers the language scaffolding and a companion cognitive layer, while four optional layers cover specific domains: a cognitive-assessment battery, generic process orchestration, large-scale data transformation, and multimodal acquisition for EEG and eye tracking. New domains plug in by writing a schema, without changing the core. The complete element catalog is in Supplementary Table S1, and a representative subset is given in @tbl-elements.

::: {#tbl-elements .list-table header-rows=1 aligns="l,l,l,l" tbl-colwidths="[33,25,11,31]"}

**A machine-readable specification.** The language is defined by a versioned LinkML schema [@moxon2025linkml], the single source of truth for element types, attribute constraints, and validation rules, which the runtime YAML schemas that the BPMN tooling reads mirror. Listing 1 gives the schema for the study container and a cognitive task: a `CognitiveTask` specializes a generic data-operation activity, requires an `instrument`, and carries an inline `configurations` block. Listing 2 shows how a research gateway maps onto BPMN. A `RandomGateway` and an `EligibilityGateway` are both specializations of a standard `bpmn:ExclusiveGateway`, so they serialize and render as ordinary BPMN gateways while carrying the attributes that make randomization and eligibility explicit. A diagram that uses them stays valid BPMN 2.0 and degrades gracefully as above. The on-disk XML form of these elements appears where the worked example encodes its n-back task (Listing 3).

**Listing 1.** Studyflow language specification (LinkML excerpt; descriptions abridged). The schema fixes element types, required attributes, and validation rules independently of any tool.

```yaml
Study:
  class_uri: bpmn:Process
  tree_root: true
  attributes:
    name:
      range: string
      required: true
    version:
      range: string
    authors:
      range: string
      multivalued: true
    runtime:
      range: RuntimeEnum

CognitiveTask:
  is_a: DataOperationActivity        # a specialized BPMN activity
  class_uri: cognitive:CognitiveTask
  attributes:
    instrument:                      # psychopy, jspsych, labjs, ...
      range: string
      required: true
    configurations:                  # instrument-specific, inline YAML
      range: YAMLString
```

**Listing 2.** Two research gateways, each a specialization of `bpmn:ExclusiveGateway` (runtime schema excerpt; abridged). The diagram stays valid BPMN while the extension carries the randomization and eligibility semantics.

```yaml
- name: RandomGateway
  superClass:
    - bpmn:ExclusiveGateway
    - bpmn:BaseElement
  properties:
    - name: algorithm
      type: AssignmentAlgorithmEnum
      default: probabilistic
    - name: probabilityFunction
      type: String
      default: uniform
- name: EligibilityGateway
  superClass:
    - bpmn:ExclusiveGateway
    - bpmn:BaseElement
  properties:
    - name: inclusionCriteria
      type: MarkdownString
      isMany: true
    - name: exclusionCriteria
      type: MarkdownString
      isMany: true
```

## 2.2 The Studyflow Modeler

The **Studyflow Modeler** is an open-source web application (MIT-licensed) that implements the Studyflow language for authoring, inspecting, simulating, and publishing diagrams. It runs entirely in the browser, with no server dependency. Two design choices shape the modeler. First, the language specification is kept as a versioned LinkML schema [@moxon2025linkml] that is independent of the modeler codebase, so third-party tools (linters, converters, execution engines) can target the same specification; the modeler tracks the schema rather than owning it. Second, the user interface is **schema-driven**: the palette entries, the inspector panel, and the validation rules are all generated from the layered moddle schemas. Adding an element type or attribute to a schema updates the interface automatically, which keeps the modeler lightweight as the notation evolves with community feedback.

The authoring workflow (Figure 3) draws on schema-driven capabilities that matter for a study. Selecting an element opens an inspector sidebar whose fields come from the element's schema entry: required attributes are flagged, enumerated values become dropdowns, and conditional attributes appear only when their condition holds. A simulation mode steps through the diagram interactively, runs the gateway logic, and shows the next allowed elements, which helps catch dead branches and missing conditions before a study runs. Export to PNG and SVG produces publication-ready figures, and the SVGs embed the source XML, so the exported figure is the runnable file. Publishing uploads the diagram to our data server [@bds], which builds its own participant-facing interface from the diagram structure; each publish creates a new server-side version, so studies already in the field do not break when authors push updates, and earlier versions stay reachable by identifier.

This separation between the specification (the LinkML schema), the authoring tool (the modeler), the runtime interface (the data server), and the visual layout (export artifacts) lets each component evolve on its own, while a single `.studyflow` source ties them together.

## 2.3 The Studyflow Runner

The **Studyflow Runner** is a separate client-side application that takes a Studyflow diagram and walks a participant (or an artificial agent) through it node by node. It lives alongside the modeler. A diagram can reach it in three ways: from the modeler's *Run* button, through a URL parameter when the diagram is hosted somewhere, or by direct file upload. An optional random seed makes branching deterministic, so the control flow of pilot runs and regression tests is reproducible.

After loading, the runner parses the diagram, validates it node by node, and traverses it from start to end. Each node the runner visits becomes a step that it renders and waits to complete; when the run reaches the end event, it finishes and applies any completion code or redirect the diagram specifies.

**Validation in layers.** Type-level constraints (required attributes, enumerated values, conditional visibility) are checked at parse time; structural constraints (every start has an outgoing flow, every gateway is fully wired, every flow has a valid source and target) are checked by the modeler at edit time; and per-step validators (a questionnaire needs an instrument, a cognitive task needs a paradigm identifier) run before traversal begins. The same per-step validators are also used by the modeler's lint pass, so authors see the errors they would see at run time.

**Gateway semantics.** Random gateways pick an outgoing branch uniformly at random, controlled by the seed. Stratified allocation currently falls back to the same uniform pick; balanced stratification is left for future work. Exclusive and inclusive gateways evaluate conditions against a runtime variable store that nodes can write to as they run, and they fall back to a default branch when no condition matches. Parallel gateways are not yet supported.

**Built-in step kinds.** Six step kinds ship: a **start** node that shows a consent screen when one is attached, an **end** node that issues a completion code and an optional redirect, an **instruction** node that displays markdown, a **questionnaire** node with built-in instruments (PHQ-9, GAD-7, BDI-II) plus custom instruments defined by an inline schema, a **cognitive-task** node that administers a task from the battery and supports three response sources (a built-in bot, runner-side uniform random, or a language-model call per trial), and a **generic-task** fallback. Elements that are not steps in the participant flow (data references, model-only sub-processes) are skipped at run time, because they matter for modeling and analysis rather than execution.

**Runtime extensibility.** New step kinds plug in by adding one folder to the runner's node directory: a small matcher selects which diagram elements the kind handles, a mapper extracts the runtime parameters from the element, and a React component renders the step. A domain group can therefore ship a custom step (an eye-tracking calibration, a VR scene) without forking the runner.

**A matter of scope.** The runner's current gaps are choices of scope rather than limits of the language, because the diagram is fully expressive at modeling time; they are consolidated in §4.4.

Figure 4 walks a participant from consent through an instruction, a questionnaire, and a cognitive task to the end screen, all on the same diagram authored in §2.2 [FILL: runner screenshots from the seed-42 walkthrough].

## 2.4Multiple views: Study / Gantt / Checklist / Figure

Each of these views is a projection $\pi_{\text{view}}$ over the formal object of §2.1 that keeps the nodes, edges, and attributes a given audience needs and drops the rest, so the Gantt view keeps the nodes whose $\lambda$ carries an `onset` or `duration` and lays them on a time axis while the Study view sets those temporal attributes aside.

A single `.studyflow` source can be rendered in four ways, each suited to a different stakeholder need (Figure 5). All the views read the same file, so changes propagate automatically.

**Study view.** The default rendering is a BPMN-like graph that shows every element and connection. The Study view is *structural*: it shows what happens and in what order, but it does not commit to wall-clock timing. It is the standard view for Methods sections, for reviewers checking the logical structure, and for pipeline authors wiring up data flow.

**Gantt view.** A Gantt-style rendering places time-sensitive elements along a time axis. BPMN has timer events but no native way to express activity duration, scheduled onset, or progress. Studyflow attaches these as optional attributes on BPMN activities and events: **onset**, **duration**, and **progress** (percentage or label). Resource allocation is expressed directly as BPMN pools and lanes, which the Gantt uses to group rows; there is no separate `resourceAllocation` attribute. When these temporal attributes are present, the Gantt view renders the diagram automatically. The same mechanism scales from trial-level timing (stimulus duration, ITI, response window) to study-level timing (visit schedule, follow-ups), with milestones as zero-duration elements and hierarchical Gantt structures mapping onto BPMN sub-processes. The Gantt view is useful for longitudinal studies and for SPIRIT-style schedules of enrolment and assessment [@spirit2013].

**Checklist view.** This task-oriented view flattens the diagram into a list of activities with their items and status. Every Studyflow element carries an optional `checklist` attribute (a markdown list) that the Checklist view extracts and aggregates. The view supports two uses: *running studies day-to-day* (what is next, what is done) and *adhering to reporting guidelines* (CONSORT, SPIRIT, STROBE, PRISMA, CARE). For the second use, guideline items map to the diagram elements that satisfy them, so a study can be audited without leaving the diagram. Checklists ship with the `.studyflow` file and can be exported to JSON or Markdown for external task managers.

**Figure view.** The Figure view renders a diagram as a publication-ready SVG in which per-element annotations decide what is shown or hidden. A manuscript figure usually needs a curated subset of the full diagram: the protocol without the data layer, or a single highlighted path through a branch. Instead of redrawing the diagram by hand, an author marks elements to show or hide and exports the curated SVG. The exported SVG embeds the complete `.studyflow` source as metadata, so the published figure is the runnable file itself rather than a picture of the study: a reader can lift the source back out, open it in the modeler, and re-run it. Because the visibility annotations live in the same `extensionElements` slot as the rest of the vocabulary, the figure stays valid BPMN and stays tied to the study it depicts. This is the mechanism behind the published CONSORT figure in §3.5.

::: {.list-table header-rows=1 aligns="l,l" tbl-colwidths="[65,35]"}
- - If you need to communicate...
  - Use

- - Procedural structure, branching, data flow
  - Study view

- - Wall-clock timing, schedules, durations
  - Gantt view

- - Coverage against a reporting checklist or protocol
  - Checklist view

- - A publication figure with selected elements shown or hidden
  - Figure view
:::

A single `.studyflow` source therefore supports four ways of reading it (a methods diagram, a project schedule, a reporting audit, and a publication figure), without forcing authors to maintain four separate documents.

# 3. A complete study, from protocol to publication

The framework of Section 2 makes a set of claims about what one artifact can be at once, and the purpose of this section is to exercise those claims end to end and to show that requirements R1 through R7 hold when a real study is run rather than only described. The walkthrough is a demonstration of the framework, and it is subordinate to it. We are not reporting a finding about agents, and the reader should not read the numbers below as an experimental result.

The study we use is a single registered human-and-agent agreement trial in which ten people and a cohort of artificial agents are co-subjects across the same six-construct objective space, allocated to a self-paced path and a time-pressured path. It is chosen because it stresses every part of the framework in one file: a registered protocol with consent and randomization, a topology that a runner actually walks, control flow and typed data on one canvas, optional domain layers over a tool-independent schema, and one enroll-allocate-run-analyze topology into which a person and an agent enter at the same nodes. The agent-cohort table (@tbl-agents) and the accuracy and response-time figures carry [FILL: values from the seed-42 runs], so the walkthrough shows the shape of the result the framework produces rather than the result itself.

The lifecycle runs in five stages: design the trial and its reporting scaffolding (§3.1), enroll and run every co-subject through one diagram (§3.2), measure agreement off the shared table (§3.3), model that agreement in the same notation (§3.4), and report against the guideline that shaped the design (§3.5). The same `.studyflow` file is the only input at every stage, so each stage reads or extends the one artifact that the stage before it left, and no view is reconstructed from a separate document.

## 3.1 Design: a registered human/agent agreement

Our worked example is a single study that enrolls ten human participants and a cohort of artificial agents as co-subjects, administers the same battery of cognitive tasks to all of them, and asks an agreement question: across the six cognitive constructs the battery probes, do the people and the agents reach approximate agreement, and where do they diverge. We design it as a registered randomized controlled trial so that this comparison is trustworthy before it runs. Each subject is allocated to one of two paths, a self-paced path and a time-pressured path, with task order counterbalanced within each path, so the two paths act as a condition slice that tests whether agreement is robust under a timing manipulation. The protocol then carries the scaffolding a registered study needs: consent, eligibility screening, seed-controlled random allocation to the two paths, and the structure a journal will later expect.

In current practice this scaffolding is spread across a registry entry, an ethics PDF, a recruitment system, and a CONSORT flow diagram drawn at write-up time. None of these is a machine-readable view of the others [@moher2012; @rennie2001; @hopewell2025consort]. The flow diagram, in particular, is a participant-tracking schematic; its four standard rows are enrollment, allocation, follow-up, and analysis, and attrition counts annotate each transition. It is a *document* about the trial, and it is not the *spec* that drove it. Studyflow makes the document and the spec one file.

We start from the CONSORT 2025 reference diagram that ships with the modeler; authors can fork it, parameterize it, and run it as the actual protocol of a new trial [@hopewell2025consort]. Figure 6 compares three artifacts: (a) the standard CONSORT 2025 reference flow as published by the CONSORT group, (b) a Studyflow reproduction encoded with the same labels and pathways, and (c) an annotated comparison whose left path uses Studyflow boundary error events and whose right path uses the traditional text-and-box treatment.

The key mechanical difference is how attrition is represented. In the traditional figure, each "Excluded / Did not receive / Lost to follow-up / Discontinued" box is an unconnected annotation that sits next to the column of follow-up activities, and readers must infer that these counts subtract from the main flow. In the Studyflow diagram, attrition is encoded as a *boundary error event* attached to the activity that participants left from. Exclusion at screening hangs off the eligibility gateway, non-receipt of intervention off the two allocation tasks, loss to follow-up and discontinuation off the follow-up tasks, and exclusion from analysis off the analysis tasks. Each event ends in an error end event with a labeled count. This has three consequences. First, the diagram's topology now matches the trial's topology, so a participant lost during follow-up exits along an edge that starts at the follow-up activity itself, rather than an arrow drawn from a side annotation. Second, summing attrition becomes a graph operation instead of a manual exercise, so a Studyflow-aware validator can check that no row's outbound counts exceed its inbound count. Third, the boundary error event is the same primitive that BPMN uses to model interrupts in any business process, so the diagram stays valid BPMN 2.0 and inherits the standard execution semantics for error handling [@stroppi2011; @ait2024bpmn_humanagent].

In the file, each attrition path is a few lines of standard BPMN: a boundary error event attached to the activity that participants leave from, wired to an error end event that carries the count.

```xml
<bpmn2:boundaryEvent id="Dropout" name="Dropped out (n=...)"
                     attachedToRef="Battery">
  <bpmn2:outgoing>Flow_Dropout_Excluded</bpmn2:outgoing>
  <bpmn2:errorEventDefinition id="ErrorDef_Dropout" />
</bpmn2:boundaryEvent>
```

The diagram carries domain semantics alongside the BPMN structure. The enrollment start event references a participant-facing consent PDF, so a runner that reaches this node renders the consent screen automatically, before any randomization happens. The screening task carries a markdown checklist (demographic intake, medical history, baseline cognitive screen) that also drives the Checklist view. The eligibility gateway and the randomization gateway are typed as such, and each task in the battery declares itself as a cognitive task with its own inline parameter block (for the n-back: the N level, stimulus duration, inter-trial interval, and trials per block). The allocation, follow-up, and analysis tasks each carry their own checklists that describe protocol obligations. A single file therefore serves four readers at once: the trial registry (a registered protocol with explicit randomization and eligibility criteria), the ethics board (consent content and per-task checklists), the data-collection platform (the embedded cognitive-task instrument and its parameters), and the journal (the CONSORT figure with attrition flows already wired). The mechanism is BPMN's standard extension protocol [@stroppi2011]: each reader interprets the layer it cares about. The union of those layers, rendered together, *is* a CONSORT diagram.

Where CONSORT structures the *report*, SPIRIT structures the *plan*. The same study also renders as a SPIRIT 2025 schedule of enrolment and assessment, based on a worked SPIRIT template that the modeler ships. Its 34 checklist items across 9 topics map onto the Gantt view [@chan2025spirit; @spirit2013]. A SPIRIT plan and a CONSORT report are then the same file at two points in its lifecycle: the schedule before randomization, and the flow diagram with attrition counts written into the labels of the boundary error events once the study has run.

Because the executor is a runtime parameter, the same flow enrolls, allocates, follows up, and analyzes an agent exactly where it does a person, mapping enrollment, eligibility, allocation, follow-up, and attrition onto an agent run as §3.2 details. CONSORT and SPIRIT originate in human trials, and reading agents as co-subjects in one flow is a deliberate extension that the unified representation makes natural, since a run that crashes or falls out of set leaves the trial along the same edge a participant lost to follow-up does.

## 3.2 Enroll and run: one diagram runs the trial for every subject

This stage enrolls and runs both kinds of co-subject, the ten people and the cohort of artificial agents, through one diagram, and it makes Studyflow's central idea concrete: *who executes the protocol is a runtime decision rather than a property of the diagram*. The participants and the agents therefore traverse the identical enroll, allocate, run, and analyze topology and write into one schema-conformant table, which is what later lets their agreement and divergence be read row for row.

**The battery.** Our study administers a six-task battery from Behaverse, a cognitive assessment battery we used, spanning working memory (n-back and digit span), attention (multiple-object tracking), processing speed (pattern comparison), fluid reasoning (matrix reasoning), and set-shifting (card sorting). These six constructs are the objective space across which the people and the agents are compared. One `.studyflow` source drives every task and every actor. The n-back serves as the worked example below, a near-universal probe of working memory [@owen2005nback], and the other five use the same machinery.

**The round-trip: enroll, allocate, and follow up.** We built the battery in the Studyflow Modeler and saved it as one Studyflow diagram. This single source orchestrates the four CONSORT stages for both paths: enrollment through consent and baseline questionnaires, an eligibility gateway, randomized allocation to two paths (self-paced and time-pressured), and follow-up through a sequence of the six tasks. Each task sits in the diagram as a cognitive-task node, and task order is counterbalanced within each path. Each task is itself a timeline of blocks: a warm-up, the test blocks, and any adaptive staircase, so the battery is a nested structure that prose and slides flatten but the diagram keeps explicit. We then loaded that file into the Studyflow Runner. The runner checks that every task's required parameters are present before traversal begins, and then walks the diagram one node at a time (Figure 4). Instructions are shown as markdown, the questionnaire before the task uses a built-in instrument (PHQ-9, GAD-7, and BDI-II all ship, and custom instruments are accepted through an inline schema), and trial-level execution is handled by the cognitive-task node. The same seed-controlled random gateway allocates every subject: seeded randomization, set as a URL parameter (`?seed=42`), fixes the path assignment, the within-task stimulus order, and every random branch, so the protocol a participant or an agent encounters is identical across runs at a given seed. Responses are a separate matter: human and language-model responses are sampled rather than fixed by the seed, so we record the seed together with the model identity and version, and we report agent results as run-level aggregates rather than as a single canonical trace.

**Encoding the trials.** Figure 7 places the traditional slide-style N-back figure next to the Studyflow equivalent. The slide is intuitive but underspecified: timing values often live only in the caption, the boundary between trial and block stays implicit, and decisions like "what counts as a correct match" are buried in the analysis code. Studyflow instead encodes the trial as an explicit subgraph, built from a stimulus activity, a boundary timer for the response window, a second boundary timer for the inter-trial interval, and text annotations that label the target and non-target branches. The trial-by-trial encoding in Figure 7 is illustrative. For runs beyond a handful of trials, the same logic compresses into a single cognitive task. Its inline configuration declares the N level, stream specification, trial count, stimulus duration, and inter-trial interval, and the runner expands it into individual trials. Listing 3 shows how these primitives are serialized in the `.studyflow` file. The same compression applies to every task in the battery: each one is a cognitive-task node whose inline timeline, blocks, stop rules, and optional staircase the runner expands into trials. Each trial the runner emits is logged to our trials schema (BDM [@bdm]), which is Psych-DS-compatible [@psychds], so the same diagram produces a CSV whose columns are fixed by the schema and whose meaning is fixed by the diagram, identically across all six tasks. The trials CSV can be reviewed side by side with the diagram, and a third party with only those two files can reconstruct what each row means without running the modeler.

**Listing 3.** The n-back task serialized in a `.studyflow` file (BPMN 2.0 XML, abridged). The task is a standard `bpmn:task` carrying a `cognitive:task` extension; its inline `cognitive:configurations` block declares the N level, the stimulus stream, and the timing, which the runner expands into individual trials.

```xml
<bpmn2:task id="Task_NB" name="N-back (text)">
  <bpmn2:extensionElements>
    <cognitive:task scene="NB" configMode="inline">
      <cognitive:configurations>
        NValue: 2
        Feature: Letters
        Streams:
          - StimulusValue: [3, 1, 2, 1, 3, 2, 3, 2, 1, 2, 3, 1]
        StreamSize: 12
        StimulusDisplayDuration: 0.5
        InterStimulusInterval: 1.5
      </cognitive:configurations>
    </cognitive:task>
  </bpmn2:extensionElements>
  <bpmn2:incoming>Flow_B_Start_NB</bpmn2:incoming>
  <bpmn2:outgoing>Flow_NB_DS</bpmn2:outgoing>
</bpmn2:task>
```

**One executor, many actors.** The runner administers every actor through one message-passing executor interface (Figure 8; the actor-model design and the interface signature are specified in §5.5). Per trial it sends the stimulus, the allowed responses, the timing constraint, and where a model needs it a rendered frame, and records the response and, where applicable, the response time under the common schema. Each actor keeps whatever state its kind needs behind that interface, a participant's session, an agent's policy, a recurrent hidden state, or a language model's context, so the runner never reaches inside it and the human and agent co-subjects of the trial are actors in one shared space. Any kind of agent can hold that role, because each realizes an Actor element the language already types by `actorType` (human, LLM, agent, or instrument; §2.1); this study fills the one executor with four actors, a human, a reinforcement-learning agent, a recurrent model, and a language model, the last two both carrying the agent type. The single-pass battery exchanges one message per trial, the synchronous special case the runner executes today, and the same actor abstraction extends to the multi-turn and actor-to-actor exchanges that BPMN message flows and choreography express, which the runner does not yet traverse (§4.5). The *human* actor renders each trial in a participant-facing interface and blocks until a person responds; ten participants ran the battery this way. *Reinforcement-learning agents* run through CogEnv [@ansarinia2022cogenv], which drives RL policies through the bot interface the Behaverse assessment application now exposes, so an agent meets the same stimuli, response options, and time constraints a participant does. Running a random or scripted policy through every node also validates the protocol, since it surfaces stuck states and timing edge cases before any human sits down. *Recurrent cognitive models* run through CogPonder [@ansarinia2023cogponder], our differentiable model that, built on PonderNet, learns to reproduce human accuracy and response times by controlling how long it ponders before it commits to a choice; it returns both a response and a pondered response time, so the cohort gains a process model whose latencies are predicted from the task rather than sampled from a prompt. *Language-model agents* run through a package that sends each trial to the configured model with a free-form prompt that steers a simulated participant (trait, target accuracy, mistake rate); vision-capable models additionally read the rendered frame, so the battery's spatial tasks (object tracking, matrix reasoning, card sorting), which carry no useful textual stimulus, stay tractable. If an actor replies with an answer outside the allowed set, the runner records the mismatch and falls back to a uniform random choice, so a transient failure cannot silently corrupt the dataset.

Read against the trial set up in §3.1, instantiating an executor package is the agent's enrollment record: the model identity and version are pinned and carried with every run, so an admitted run enters the trial exactly as a consented participant does. The runner's out-of-set fallback is the attrition mechanism: a run that exceeds the fallback threshold, times out, or crashes exits along a boundary error event and is counted as a dropout in the same CONSORT flow a participant lost to follow-up would be.

**The agent cohort: a matrix enrolled across the objective space.** We enroll a matrix of agents across the whole battery, rather than scoring one agent on one task, so the agents meet the same six constructs the people traverse. We cross three factors. The first is *model*: a uniform-random baseline, a recurrent cognitive model (CogPonder), a reinforcement-learning policy through CogEnv, several open-weight text models served locally through Ollama, and a commercial vision-language model (Claude). The second is *trait*: a set of response profiles drawn from prior cognitive and psychological characterizations of participants rather than chosen ad hoc, namely a careful high-accuracy responder with the conservative decision criterion the diffusion model formalizes [@ratcliff2008diffusion], a fatigued responder marked by intermittent attentional lapses [@robertson1997oops], and a speed-accuracy-tradeoff responder at the fast, error-prone end of that classic trade [@wickelgren1977sat]. The third is *task*: the six battery tasks. A trait is fixed by a free-form prompt held constant across the battery while each task supplies its own response instructions, so each model produces a profile across constructs rather than a single score; for the prompt-free model families the same axis is set natively, through the pondering cost in the recurrent model and the policy in the reinforcement-learning agent. We administered every model-by-trait-by-task cell at seed 42, fixing the stimulus order by the seed and sampling the responses. @tbl-agents reports accuracy, median response time, and the out-of-set fallback rate for every cell [FILL: values from the seed-42 runs], and Figure 9 shows the accuracy and response-time profiles across tasks [FILL: rendered from the same runs]; the random baseline sits near chance, and the open-weight models run the same battery without an external API [FILL: the observed open- versus closed-weight pattern]. This is the "few models, many items" regime [@ansarinia2022cogenv] extended across tasks: rather than rank many models on a single task, we vary the diagram (task, difficulty, response window, trait) and profile a cohort of agents over a whole battery of parametrically related items.

::: {#tbl-agents .list-table header-rows=1 aligns="l,l,l,r,r,r" tbl-colwidths="[16,16,16,16,18,18]"}

- - Model
  - Trait
  - Task
  - Accuracy
  - Median RT (ms)
  - Fallback rate

**Beyond one participant.** The same notation scales past the single-participant battery in two directions, both roadmap items for the runner (§4.5) that the diagram already expresses. When the *interaction itself* is the unit of analysis, as in joint action [@sebanz2006joint], dyadic and parent-child protocols, two-player games, and hyperscanning [@babiloni2014hyperscanning; @hakim2023interbrain], BPMN 2.0's **choreography task** models a directed exchange between participants with an explicit initiator [@pufahl2022; @decker2011choreography], while the Lab Streaming Layer aligns the multimodal streams one layer down [@kothe2025lsl]. When the subject is artificial, the agent cohort above is the same construct seen from the confederate tradition [@dahlback1993woz], now routinely filled by language models that simulate participants [@aher2023llms], are evaluated as cognitive subjects [@binz2023gpt3], or act as generative confederates [@park2023agents]; as discovery moves toward multi-agent laboratories [@ghareeb2025], the case for a machine-readable procedural specification only grows, and alignment research makes the same case from the measurement side, comparing a set of agents, humans included, across a space of objectives [@nayebi2026alignment]. A choreography task between a human and an LLM agent is the same primitive as one between two humans, and the diagram validates against the BPMN 2.0 choreography schema even though the runner does not yet traverse it [@stroppi2011].

**Reading agreement off the shared table.** The correspondence to the alignment account is exact enough to name part for part. The agent set is the cohort of agents together with the ten people, human and artificial co-subjects in one trial; the objective space is the battery of parametrically related items, the six constructs; and the schema-bound table is where approximate agreement across those objectives, or its absence, is read off. The same theory shows that once this space grows, no agent covers it uniformly, so the work shifts to budgeting measurement toward the slices that matter and to compressing many objectives into a smaller set that can be certified [@nayebi2026alignment; @nayebi2025corrigible]. Studyflow does not decide which slices or which values those should be, a question that belongs to the alignment literature; it gives an author the controls to target them, since the diagram fixes the task, difficulty, response window, and trait, the runner records the seed, the model version, and every out-of-set fallback per trial, and the choreography roadmap carries the same primitive into the multi-turn protocols that single-shot rating cannot express.

**Limits.** The scope limits of this multi-actor setup, and the boundary between what the notation expresses and what a presentation library renders, are consolidated in the Limitations discussion (§4.4).

## 3.3 Measure agreement: human-agent comparison and the CONSORT flow

Because both kinds of subject wrote to one schema-bound table, this stage reads the agreement question off that table: across the six constructs, where do the ten participants and the agent cohort reach approximate agreement, and where do they diverge. This stage also closes the CONSORT flow by counting the analysis exclusions on the same record. The analysis that produces this read-out is usually a script, an R or Python notebook whose structure (the order of operations, their dependencies, and the kind of each step) lives in code and comments rather than in a machine-readable record. Studyflow's data operations give every script-style operation an explicit type (element-wise map, row filter, partition group, group-wise reduce, expansion, generic transform, and bundled pipeline), so the *kind* of work each step does is visible in the diagram rather than implicit in the code, and together with dataset, data-store, and schema elements the diagram becomes a complete, machine-readable pre-registration of the analysis.

We analyze the trials through a typed pipeline: read the raw trials; filter invalid ones (RT < 100 ms, missing data, fallback-flagged rows), the analysis-exclusion row of the CONSORT flow, which applies one rule set to both populations so a human trial that fails QA and an agent run flagged out of set are removed at the same node and counted together; map to derived measures; branch at an exclusive gateway on the comparison of interest; group by task, actor, and trait; reduce to per-group accuracy, median RT, and standard errors; route through a manual review of outliers; and render and write the summary table and figures, each to a schema-declared dataset. Three properties are not optional: the conditional branch is visible in the topology rather than buried inside an `if`; the manual review has an explicit place in the diagram, making it harder to skip; and the schema on the output table is part of the spec rather than implicit in the column names.

Because the same diagram carries process and typed data together, the human-and-agent agreement is auditable from one artifact rather than asserted across mismatched ones; the contrast with the process-only and data-only tools that force this split is taken up in §4.2. Activities sit on the sequence-flow graph, while datasets, stores, catalogs, schemas, and snapshots sit on a parallel data-flow graph; BPMN data associations, drawn as dashed edges, connect the two. Every dataset declares its format (BDM, BIDS, Psych-DS, or generic) and a schema, inline or external; tabular data carries a CSVW body or a schema reference [@hoytO3GuidelinesOpen2024; @csvw], while non-tabular data documents tensor dimensions, dtypes, and units. Bindings to BIDS [@bids], Psych-DS [@psychds], and BDM [@bdm] are typed contracts that the modeler validates and the runner respects, rather than comments, so an analyst can confirm from the diagram alone that a downstream task consumes exactly the column an upstream task produced.

Concretely, Figure 10 shows the RT-analysis subprocess beside the equivalent dplyr code. The diagram encodes the same chained pipeline a tidyverse user would write as `filter |> mutate |> group_by |> summarize`, but it adds two commitments. First, the inputs and outputs are typed: the raw and summary datasets are typed (BDM trials level on the way in, models level on the way out), registered in a catalog, and physically stored in a backing store (a DuckDB-plus-Parquet ducklake in our example). Second, the analysis task's composed-operation marker declares which primitive operations the task may perform, so tooling can reject any implementation that touches an undeclared column or runs an unauthorized operation. The comparison this produces is the agreement read-out that enrollment and follow-up set up: accuracy and response-time distributions across task, actor, and trait, shown side by side across the six constructs. The human cohort slots into the same table and schema the agents wrote to, so the ten-participant battery and the agent cohort are compared row for row, and approximate agreement or its absence is read off the shared table.

Pre-registration of analysis then becomes the diagram itself. In current practice, a pre-registered plan is free text on a registry website, with no machine-checkable link to the code that is eventually run. Under the Studyflow encoding, the diagram is the spec and the dplyr pipeline is one valid implementation; any divergence between the two can be detected by inspecting the data-operation markers and the input and output schemas. The modeler reduces visual density with collapsible layers: the high-level protocol turns the data layer off, and the full dependency graph turns it on; whether this makes large process-plus-data diagrams more legible than the artifacts they replace is the unvalidated claim taken up in §4.4.

The worked dataset behind this pipeline is the seed-42 agent cohort together with the ten-participant human battery, both written to the same trials schema, so the table records the two cohorts enrolled in one CONSORT flow and supports the agreement read across the six constructs [FILL: summary RT values and per-construct agreement once the analysis is run].

## 3.4 Model agreement: a human-versus-agent classifier

The analysis stage reads agreement and divergence off group summaries, and the same trials can feed a model that learns the read-out: a classifier of human versus agent that locates where the two subject populations separate across the objective space, a model of the response-time distribution across tasks and difficulty levels, or, with accompanying neural recordings, a multimodal predictor. Because the ten participants and the agent cohort wrote one schema-bound table, the classifier is trained on the same rows the row-for-row comparison reads, and it is authored in the same diagram rather than in a separate codebase. ML pipelines face the same fragmentation that experimental protocols do: the model card lives in one repository, feature engineering in another, the training script in a third, the deployment config in a fourth, and retraining triggers in cron jobs that nobody can find, if they exist at all. Studyflow's data operations, gateways, and schema-bound data elements apply to ML pipelines as cleanly as to behavioral analyses; within a Studyflow, an analysis and a training pipeline share one notation with different operators [@tetzlaff2022bpmn4sml].

Beyond the classifier, the same notation expresses a full multimodal preprocessing and training pipeline that harmonizes EEG, fMRI, and behavioral recordings across heterogeneous public datasets, which we specify in Figure 11 rather than run here. It makes three properties explicit that are hard to recover from prose: provenance is the diagram, since every derived artifact traces back to its raw source through the nodes that produced it; the multiverse is first-class, with defensible analytical paths as explicit branches rather than version-controlled forks [@steegen2016multiverse]; and cross-dataset interoperability is a schema decision, so a preprocessing subprocess defined once applies to every dataset in the same format. Behavioral data is converted to BDM trials [@defossez2020bdm], the same schema the battery's agents wrote to, and the same encoding extends to containerized HPC execution and to downstream training, fine-tuning, evaluation, monitoring, and planned data-governance subprocesses [@tetzlaff2022bpmn4sml; @ghosh2025reproducible_digital_health].

## 3.5 Report: the file that ran the trial is the CONSORT figure and the benchmark

The lifecycle closes where it began, with the reporting guidelines that shaped the design. Because the trial ran inside the same file, the CONSORT figure is not redrawn at write-up time; the modeler's Figure view (§2.4) exports it from the protocol that enrolled, allocated, followed up, and analyzed the ten participants and the agent cohort, with the attrition counts for both populations already written into the boundary error events and the `.studyflow` source embedded in the SVG as metadata. The figure that appears in the paper is, literally, the file that ran the trial, so the one exported source is at once the CONSORT report and the specification of the agreement benchmark it ran. This directly addresses the artifact-drift problem that motivates this work.

Reporting against a guideline then becomes a property the diagram can be checked for, rather than a PDF assembled alongside it. Each guideline is, in structure, a controlled vocabulary, a checklist, and sometimes a flow diagram, and Studyflow handles all of them in the same way: checklist items become entries in the optional `checklist` attribute on the relevant element, flow diagrams become Studyflow renderings with boundary error events for attrition where applicable, and vocabulary becomes labels on activities, gateways, and data elements. Because the checklist attribute is machine-readable, the Checklist view shows the items as a markdown list, with each one linked back to the element that satisfies it, so a study can be audited without leaving the diagram. The EQUATOR network catalogs these standards [@simera2010equator]; @tbl-guidelines lists the eleven most widely used, together with Studyflow's current coverage. The two that ship today (CONSORT and SPIRIT) exercise the full mechanism; the entries marked Roadmap are authoring work rather than missing capability, since the elements, attributes, and Checklist view they need are already in place and each takes about half a day to template.

Two guidelines ship as worked templates today: CONSORT 2025, whose 30-item checklist [@hopewell2025consort] maps onto the shipped template, and SPIRIT 2025, whose 34 items across 9 topics [@chan2025spirit] map onto a Gantt view (Figure 12) that serves as both schedule and checklist. The pattern recurs across the catalog, with STROBE and PRISMA next: PRISMA 2020 [@page2021prisma] standardized the study-flow diagrams that are visual instances of what Studyflow generalizes, TIDieR [@hoffmann2014tidier] makes intervention details first-class items that map onto the participant branch, and ARRIVE 2.0 [@percie2020arrive], with its history of endorsement without adherence, supplies the animal-research counterpart.

Reporting guidelines and execution specifications need not be different artifacts. At publication, the manuscript ships three artifacts that are all views of one source: the exported figure that is at once the CONSORT report and the benchmark specification, the Checklist-view audit against the target guideline, and the `.studyflow` file itself, paired with the schema-conformant trials table that holds both subject populations. From these, a reader can reconstruct what every element and every column means, and read where the people and the agents agree across the battery and where they diverge, without rerunning the trial.
