# 4. Discussion

## 4.1 What Studyflow changes: from divergent artifacts to one auditable diagram

Current practice keeps the *protocol*, the *pipeline*, and the *figure* as three separate artifacts. They begin in agreement, and over a project's life they drift apart. Studyflow consolidates these into a single source-of-truth file. One CONSORT diagram is, at the same time, the participant-flow figure, the spec a reviewer audits against the checklist, and the runnable artifact that the runner steps through. The battery is the protocol text, the trial-loop logic, and the executable tasks. The response time pipeline is both the analysis section and the transformation script. Because there is only one source, these views can no longer drift apart. Several things follow. One source is read at different zoom levels: an ethics reviewer, a collaborator, and an engineer read the same diagram, the Study view for procedural structure, the Gantt for timing, and the Checklist for guideline compliance. The artifact is plain BPMN 2.0 XML with stable identifiers, so it diffs cleanly in Git and embeds inside an SVG export, bringing procedural specifications under the same review and version-control discipline that already governs data and code. The specification is independent of the tool, a LinkML schema maintained separately from the modeler that third-party linters, converters, and renderers can target directly. Process and data live on one diagram, where data artifacts and data operations sit alongside the procedure that produced them and community-schema bindings (BIDS, Psych-DS, BDM, CSVW) attach to specific tasks. Reporting-guideline conformance becomes a diagram property, since checklist items, vocabulary, and flow diagrams from guidelines such as CONSORT, SPIRIT, STROBE, and PRISMA map directly to elements of the diagram and are checkable in the source file itself.

One protocol, many actors, so a human-and-agent agreement trial becomes one auditable artifact. Because execution is a runtime decision, the same source runs human participants, classic reinforcement-learning agents, recurrent cognitive models, and language-model agents as actors behind one executor interface. The worked example uses this property to author one registered randomized controlled trial in which the ten people and the agent cohort are co-subjects, passing through the identical enroll, allocate, run, and analyze topology and summarized into one schema-conformant table where agreement and divergence are read off row for row. This is the practical pathway that alignment research calls for from the measurement side, the mechanism design of benchmarks and interactive protocols in which a set of agents, humans included, is compared across a space of objectives [@nayebi2026alignment; @nayebi2025corrigible]. The claim stays at the level of notation, that Studyflow can author such a benchmark and that the six constructs are its objective space and not safety values. A benchmark for AI systems no longer needs to be written three times in three formats; the protocol stays one artifact.

One property underlies them all: reproducibility becomes a feature of the shared artifact rather than of documentation maintained separately from it. The diagram an ethics board approves is the diagram participants and agents run, and it is the diagram the figures come from, so the comparison between people and agents is auditable from one source rather than asserted across mismatched artifacts. Because the specification and its executions share a single source, we expect Studyflow to compose with existing reproducibility infrastructure rather than to compete with it.

## 4.2 Relationship to existing ecosystems

Studyflow sits at the intersection of four ecosystems, and it does not aim to replace any of them.

**Execution stacks.** A whole family of engines solves a problem Studyflow leaves alone: scalable, reproducible execution on heterogeneous compute, among them Nextflow, the Common Workflow Language (CWL), the Workflow Description Language (WDL), Pegasus, Apache Airflow, Kedro, NiPype, and Pydra [@zhao2008scientific_workflows; @cuevasvicenttin2013workflows; @nextflow; @cwl; @pydra]. Their representations target machines and developers, not ethics boards and journal reviewers, and they model a workflow as a directed acyclic graph (DAG), which fits data pipelines with fixed inputs and outputs. Much of scientific inquiry is iterative, however, and BPMN expresses its feedback loops directly through sequence flows, boundary events, and choreography [@ghareeb2025], whereas a DAG emulates them through external control logic or repeated executions. The two designs are complementary: Studyflow sits *above* such systems, since a task can reference an external script (a Nextflow process, a Kedro node, or a NiPype workflow) and a downstream tool can compile the protocol-level diagram into an executable graph for one of these engines [@ghosh2025reproducible_digital_health]. By the same logic, Studyflow leaves process-mining on runtime traces to other tools, which can consume its trace structure directly [@vanderaalst2016process].

**Data standards.** BIDS, Psych-DS, and CSVW prescribe how datasets are structured but say nothing about the process that produced them [@bids; @psychds; @csvw]. Studyflow describes that process and references these standards, with our own Behaverse Data Model [@bdm], through schema-bound dataset, table, and schema elements: a BIDS-typed dataset linked to a "Record EEG" task tells reader and machine both *what* was collected and *how*.

**Reporting guidelines.** CONSORT, SPIRIT, STROBE, and STARD, with their siblings, enforce structure at the publication stage [@moher2012; @spirit2013; @strobe; @stard], and today conformance is checked by hand against PDF supplements. Authored as Studyflow, a guideline carries its checklist items as elements, so conformance becomes a property the diagram can be checked against rather than a separate checklist.

**Other BPMN profiles.** BPMN4CP for clinical pathways [@braun2014], BPMN4sML for serverless ML [@tetzlaff2022bpmn4sml], and the human-agent extension [@ait2024bpmn_humanagent] are sibling profiles in adjacent domains, and Studyflow's layered architecture follows the same pattern, so future extensions for neuroimaging, clinical neurology, or developmental research can layer in without modifying the core. Visual modeling languages already used in life-sciences-adjacent fields, such as Systems Biology Graphical Notation [@novere2009], confirm both the appetite for graphical formalization and the importance of domain-specific vocabulary [@norouzi2025semantic_processes].

Just as Studyflow does not aim to replace these ecosystems, it is not an ontology of experimental design. Process ontologies are numerous, but they tend to have high upfront cost and low reuse [@norouzi2025semantic_processes]. We have aimed instead for a profile small enough to learn from one worked example and a glossary, and enforced by tooling rather than by inspection.

A shared architectural pattern across several adjacent systems makes Studyflow's position concrete. LinkML [@moxon2025linkml], NIDM-Results [@maumet2016nidm], BIDS [@bids], and ARTEM-IS [@styles2021artemis; @soskic2025artemis] share one pattern but occupy *different planes* of it. The pattern has a schema layer, a human-friendly authoring layer, and one or more machine-readable outputs, and each system covers a different aspect of a study: LinkML over the data model, NIDM-Results over analysis outputs, BIDS over multimodal data organization, and ARTEM-IS over methods reporting. The procedural plane of this pattern, an end-to-end, machine-readable, human-authorable specification of the study *process*, is the gap that Studyflow fills. ARTEM-IS is the closest existing precedent in spirit: it commits the EEG-methods reporting community to structured templates that emit both human-readable forms and JSON. Studyflow generalizes the same commitment, from EEG-methods reporting to whole-study procedural specification. Concrete interoperability follows naturally from this framing: Studyflow diagrams can emit NIDM-Results-compatible analysis sub-graphs, schema-bind `Dataset` elements to BIDS layouts, express their data plane in LinkML, and export their methods-reporting block as ARTEM-IS-compatible JSON. None of these crosswalks subsumes a neighbor; the value is mutual.

## 4.3 Objections and alternate views

A profile that spans protocol, execution, analysis, and publication invites objections from both of its intended audiences, and we take the strongest ones in turn rather than wait for them at review. Each is stated as a skeptic would state it, and each answer concedes what is true before saying what is left standing.

**"BPMN is heavyweight, and this is one more notation to learn."** This is a fair cost, and we do not claim it away. A reader new to flowcharts still faces a learning curve, and we argue only that it is a gentler one than a custom language would impose, because BPMN's visual grammar is already recognized across engineering and analysis [@white2004introduction; @moody2009physics]. We also keep the surface small on purpose: the always-loaded layers are the language core and a companion cognitive layer, and everything else is an optional domain layer that a given study never has to open (Table S1). The bet is that one worked example and a glossary are enough to start, and a readability study is the proper test of that bet (§4.4).

**"This is just a flowchart with extra labels."** A box-and-arrow figure communicates at a glance, and Studyflow keeps that affordance on purpose. The difference is that the same artifact is executable rather than only descriptive (R2): a runner walks the file a reviewer reads, stable identifiers let it diff in Git and embed in an SVG export (R1), and the elements validate against a versioned LinkML schema so that *cognitive task*, *random gateway*, and *eligibility check* carry checkable meaning rather than informal labels [@moxon2025linkml]. A flowchart that an ethics board reads, a participant runs, and a figure exports from one source is doing more than a flowchart, and the added structure is what earns the difference.

**"Reading artificial agents as co-subjects in a CONSORT trial overclaims; CONSORT is for human trials."** We agree that CONSORT was written for human randomized trials, and we do not assert that an agent cohort inherits the ethical or inferential standing of a human cohort. The claim is narrower and stays at the level of notation: the enroll, allocate, run, and analyze topology is one shape, and because the executor is a runtime decision rather than a property of the diagram (R7), the same shape can route a human cohort and an agent cohort into one schema-conformant table where agreement and divergence are read off row for row. The six constructs are the objective space of that read and not safety values, and the alignment account that motivates it supplies the framing rather than a proof that the agents are subjects in the human sense [@nayebi2026alignment; @nayebi2025corrigible]. What we demonstrate is that Studyflow can author such a benchmark, and the standing of the agent cohort remains a question for the alignment and ethics literatures.

**"A single source of truth is brittle and risks tool lock-in."** A single source does concentrate risk, and the design answers that concern directly rather than deny it. The specification is a LinkML schema maintained separately from the modeler, so third-party linters, converters, and renderers can target it without depending on any single application (R6), and the artifact on disk is plain BPMN 2.0 XML that opens in any compliant tool and degrades gracefully when a tool does not know the domain extensions (R4) [@white2004introduction; @magnani2009bpdmn]. The modeler is one open-source client of that schema and not the schema itself, so a project that abandons our tooling keeps a valid, tool-independent file. Single source is a property of the schema-bound artifact, and it is what lets the views stop drifting, so we treat the concentration as the feature and the tool-independence as the safeguard.

**"Without a readability study, the single-source legibility benefit is asserted rather than shown."** This is correct, and we state it plainly as a limitation rather than argue around it. We have not yet measured how legible large process-plus-data diagrams are, compared with the artifacts they replace, and the legibility claim (R3) is therefore a design goal that a study has still to test (§4.4). What the modeler offers in the meantime is a mechanism rather than evidence: collapsible layers let the high-level protocol turn the data layer off and the full dependency graph turn it on, so density is a reader's choice. The comprehension question itself we leave to a readability study with cognitive scientists, and until then we do not present the benefit as measured.

**"Why not an ontology, or why not just extend an execution engine?"** These are the two natural alternatives, and Studyflow sits deliberately between them. We did not build an ontology of experimental design because process ontologies tend to carry high upfront cost and see low reuse, so we aimed instead at a profile small enough to learn from one worked example and a glossary, enforced by tooling rather than by inspection [@norouzi2025semantic_processes]. We also did not extend an execution engine, because that family targets scalable execution on heterogeneous compute for machines and developers, an audience that excludes ethics boards and journal reviewers, and it models a workflow as a directed acyclic graph that emulates the loops and multi-party exchanges of experimental procedure only through external control logic [@nextflow; @cwl; @pydra]. Studyflow prioritizes communication and process and data on one canvas (R5), and it sits above such engines: a task can reference an external Nextflow process or NiPype workflow, and a downstream tool can compile the protocol-level diagram into an executable graph for one of them. The boundary is the point, and it is why the profile is neither a heavy ontology nor another runtime.

## 4.4 Limitations

The scope limits of the current system fall into two kinds, and we keep them apart because conflating them would misstate what the language can express. The first kind is a choice of scope in the *tooling*, where the diagram is fully expressive at modeling time and each gap corresponds to a roadmap item. The Studyflow Runner ships a fixed set of step kinds, does not support parallel gateways, falls back to a uniform pick where balanced stratified allocation is called for, and does not yet traverse choreography tasks, although the diagram that declares them validates against the BPMN 2.0 choreography schema [@stroppi2011]. The multi-actor setup likewise works today for the Behaverse battery, the 22 tasks recognized by our data server, CogEnv, CogPonder, and the runner; a custom PsychoPy [@peirce2019psychopy] or jsPsych task referenced from a diagram still runs for human participants, but the reinforcement-learning, recurrent-model, and language-model adapters would each need a matching bridge to read its stimulus stream and inject responses. None of these is a limit of the notation, and generalizing the trial-level interface beyond this battery is a roadmap item.

The second kind is a deliberate boundary of *what Studyflow is for* rather than a missing feature. Studyflow is a specification of the study process and not a stimulus-presentation library, so rendering letters at a fixed retinal angle still requires the assessment battery itself or an external framework reached by URL; the diagram describes which stimulus to show, in what order, under what timing constraint, and what to record, and the pixel-level mechanics are left to the presentation software. Some designs are also intrinsically awkward to express as directed graphs, including adaptive trials, certain Bayesian sequential designs, and ABAB single-subject designs that need feedback, dynamic re-allocation, or open-ended replay; the choreography and message-flow elements reach some of this, and the rest is current research.

Two claims central to the paper remain unvalidated, and we mark them as such. We have not yet measured the legibility of large process-plus-data diagrams against the protocol PDFs, manuscript flow figures, and analysis scripts they replace, so the single-source comprehension benefit (R3) is a design goal awaiting a readability study. Adoption beyond our own group is still limited, and although the tooling ships MIT-licensed and browser-only, with BPMN 2.0 XML on disk, LinkML as the source of truth, and no server dependency, external uptake is a goal rather than a result; the concrete signals we will watch for are set out among the future directions (§4.5). These are the honest edges of the contribution, and naming them is part of the contribution.

## 4.5 Future directions

The language and tooling leave room to grow, and the layered design keeps each addition incremental. On the data side, the vocabulary could gain timeseries and event-marker structures, storage and data-governance operations, and a broader tidyverse-style operator set. On the tooling side, a data-store schema editor, richer inspector ergonomics, and further worked examples sit on the roadmap. Runner support for parallel gateways, stratified allocation, and choreography traversal is also planned, and in time a diagram could drive downstream execution stacks such as Kedro, Nextflow, or NiPype. Beyond these incremental additions, the same line of work points toward authoring auditable human-and-agent agreement benchmarks at a larger scale, since stratified allocation and choreography traversal would carry the present single-pass battery into the multi-turn and interactive protocols it does not yet reach. We describe these as open directions; none has shipped yet.

A larger question is community formation. Sibling BPMN profiles in clinical pathways and serverless ML emerged because a small number of groups committed to the same notation, and Studyflow's layered design is deliberately set up to make new domain extensions cheap, each one being a single schema file plus optional renderer code. The adoption signals we watch for are forks of the modeler for adjacent domains, third-party validators against the LinkML schema, and re-use of the SPIRIT and CONSORT templates in registered reports and journal supplements, and we will report these (fork counts, external data-server deployments, and third-party Studyflow files) in future work as they appear.

Two lines of empirical work would strengthen the evidence base. The first is a readability and comprehension study with 5-10 cognitive scientists. It would compare Studyflow diagrams against the artifacts they replace: protocol PDFs, manuscript flow figures, and analysis scripts. This would test directly whether the single-source design measurably reduces reviewer effort. The second is a set of end-to-end demonstrations beyond the single study reported here: a multi-session longitudinal study, an ABAB single-subject design, an MLOps pipeline with a fairness audit and retraining loop, and a human-and-agent agreement benchmark that enrolls people and a cohort of agents as co-subjects in one registered flow and reads their agreement and divergence across the objective space off one schema-bound table. Each one would map the boundaries of what the current vocabulary covers, and the agreement benchmark in particular would test whether the CONSORT-grade enroll, allocate, run, and analyze topology holds beyond the single battery reported here. Both are realistic for a follow-up applications paper once Studyflow has been picked up by groups outside our own.

# 5. Methods

The framework section (§2.1 to §2.4) describes what Studyflow is and how its three artifacts behave from a user's point of view. This section gives the implementation and specification detail behind that account: the layered schema that defines the language, the on-disk serialization, the formal grammar, the internal structure of the modeler and the runner, and the conventions that make a run reproducible. Each subsection cross-references the framework rather than restating it, so the specification lives here and the main argument stays forward-moving.

## 5.1 The language specification

The Studyflow language is defined once and projected into the format each tool needs. The single source of truth is a versioned LinkML schema [@moxon2025linkml] that fixes the element types, attribute constraints, and validation rules of §2.1 independently of any tool; it exists as two copies, one bundled with the modeler at `studyflow-modeler/src/assets/schemas/studyflow.linkml.yaml` and a standalone copy at `schemas/studyflow/schema.linkml.yaml`. Its header declares the prefixes that bind Studyflow to the host standard and the community data models: `bpmn` for the BPMN metamodel, `studyflow` and `cognitive` for the two always-loaded layers, and `bids`, `psychds`, `bdm`, and `csvw` for the data bindings. Keeping the specification in LinkML rather than in the modeler codebase is what makes the notation tool-independent, so a third-party linter, converter, or execution engine can target the same file the modeler tracks.

The runtime tooling reads a mirror of that source in the format the BPMN engine expects. The browser's BPMN library consumes moddle YAML schemas, so each LinkML definition is mirrored into a moddle layer that carries the same element types and attributes in the runtime form. The vocabulary is partitioned into six layers, enumerated in the modeler's `SCHEMAS` constant with an explicit `core` flag on each, which maps exactly onto the layered set of §2.1. The two `core: true` layers are `studyflow` (the study container, events, sequence flows, the base activity, and the shared data infrastructure) and its companion `cognitive` layer (cognitive tasks, video-game paradigms, rest periods, questionnaires, instructions, and the research gateways). Four optional layers load on demand: a Behaverse cognitive-assessment battery (`behaverse`), a process-orchestration library (`omniprocess`), a data-transformation library for the DataTrove ecosystem (`datatrove`), and an acquisition layer for the OpenBCI Galea VR headset (`galea`), whose `GaleaRecording` variant carries multimodal metadata spanning EEG, EMG, EOG, EDA, PPG, eye tracking, and a head IMU. Only the two core layers have LinkML mirrors; the four optional layers are authored as moddle schemas alone, which keeps the authoritative core small while still letting new domain semantics plug in.

The schemas drive everything downstream, so the documentation, the validator, and the converters are all derived rather than hand-maintained. At startup the modeler globs every `*.moddle.yaml` file, force-enables any `core` layer, and converts each through a single parser (`toModelerModdleSchema`) into the structures the palette, inspector, and validator read; the element catalog of @tbl-elements and Supplementary Table S1 is generated from the same LinkML source, and the modeler can also emit a LinkML instance from a diagram's data elements, each class carrying a `class_uri` back to its Studyflow type. Because one schema generates the interface, the documentation, and the validation, adding an element type or attribute updates all three at once.

## 5.2 Serialization

A Studyflow file on disk is a valid BPMN 2.0 document in which every domain-specific element is a standard BPMN element whose schema-specific payload nests in an `extensionElements` block, so the structure a generic BPMN tool reads is untouched. Three independent namespaces carry the extensions: `studyflow` (`http://behaverse.org/schemas/studyflow`) for the study container, the start and end events, and the data infrastructure; `cognitive` (`http://behaverse.org/schemas/studyflow/cognitive`) for the cognitive activity types and the research gateways; and the optional layers under their own URIs, for example `behaverse` (`http://behaverse.org/schemas/studyflow/behaverse`). The worked example declares exactly these three alongside the standard `bpmn2`, `bpmndi`, `dc`, and `di` namespaces. Listing 2 in §2.1 shows the moddle definition of two research gateways as specializations of `bpmn:ExclusiveGateway`, and Listing 3 shows the on-disk result for the n-back task: a plain `bpmn:task` whose `cognitive:task` extension wraps an inline `cognitive:configurations` block.

The namespaced layout is what makes graceful degradation a property of the format rather than a feature of any one reader. A generic BPMN renderer ignores the extension content it does not recognize and still draws a correct process diagram, while a Studyflow-aware tool reads, validates, and renders the same extensions consistently (§2.1). This is BPMN's standard extension protocol [@stroppi2011], so each reader interprets the layer it cares about. The study root marks itself with an empty `studyflow:study` element inside the process's `extensionElements`, which lets a Studyflow-aware reader recognize the file as a study without changing how a generic tool treats the underlying `bpmn:process`.

Two further serialization conventions support the single-source-of-truth goal. Studyflow leaves XML namespaces, element identifiers, and the base shape vocabulary untouched (§2.1), and identifiers are stable across edits, so successive versions of a diagram produce clean line-oriented diffs in Git and stay valid BPMN. Files are saved with a `.studyflow` extension to signal the extended profile while remaining ordinary BPMN 2.0 XML. Export to SVG can embed the source XML inside the image, so a single committed file is at once the publication figure and the runnable, diffable source.

## 5.3 The Studyflow grammar

The structural shape of a Studyflow diagram can also be stated as a formal grammar, independent of the XML in which it is stored. Listing 4 gives it in EBNF: a study is a labeled collection of elements and sequence flows, the admissible activity and gateway types are terminal alternatives, and the data-operation vocabulary, data elements, and choreography are productions over identifiers and typed attributes. The grammar is reference material documenting the structure the schema enforces, not a parser input, since the canonical on-disk form is the BPMN 2.0 XML of §5.2.

The grammar and the schema describe the same object from two directions: the grammar states which arrangements of elements, flows, attributes, and data associations are admissible, while the LinkML schema of §5.1 fixes each element's type and attributes. Together they pin down the typed, attributed directed graph $(N, E, T, \tau, \lambda)$ of §2.1, and a diagram is well-formed when it parses against the grammar and validates against the schema.

**Listing 4.** The Studyflow grammar in EBNF notation (included for reference; the canonical on-disk form is BPMN 2.0 XML). A study is a labeled collection of elements and sequence flows; activity and gateway types, the data-operation vocabulary, the data elements, and choreography are productions over identifiers and typed attributes.

```ebnf
/* ========== Top level ========== */
Definitions       ::= Study*
Study             ::= 'Study' Identifier Attribute* (Element | SequenceFlow)*
SubProcess        ::= 'SubProcess' Identifier Attribute* (Element | SequenceFlow | DataAssociation)*
Element           ::= Event | Activity | Gateway | SubProcess
                    | DataObject | DataCatalog | DataStorage | Dataset
                    | Schema | Array | Snapshot

/* ========== Events ========== */
Event             ::= StartEvent | EndEvent
StartEvent        ::= 'StartEvent' Identifier Attribute*    /* may carry consentFormUri */
EndEvent          ::= 'EndEvent' Identifier Attribute*      /* may carry redirectTo, completionCodeType, completionCode */

/* ========== Activities ========== */
Activity              ::= 'Activity' Identifier ActivityAttributeList Choreography?
ActivityAttributeList ::= ActivityType ActivityAttribute*
ActivityType          ::= '@type' ('CognitiveTask' | 'Questionnaire' | 'Instruction' |
                                   'Rest' | 'VideoGame' | 'BehaverseTask' |
                                   'Script' | 'Manual')
ActivityAttribute     ::= Attribute | DataInput | DataOutput | DataOperation

/* ========== Data transformations ========== */
DataOperation      ::= OpClause+
OpClause           ::= '@op' (PrimitiveOp | CompositeOp) DataInput+ DataOutput+
PrimitiveOp        ::= 'Transform' | 'Map' | 'Filter' | 'FlatMap' | 'Reduce' | 'Group'
CompositeOp        ::= 'Compose' PrimitiveOp+

/* ========== Data elements ========== */
DataCatalog        ::= 'DataCatalog' Identifier Attribute*               /* url */
DataStorage        ::= 'DataStorage' Identifier Attribute*               /* persistent physical store */
Dataset            ::= 'Dataset' Identifier Attribute*                   /* catalog, storage, schema, format */
Schema             ::= 'Schema' Identifier Attribute*                    /* format, body */
Array              ::= 'Array' Identifier Attribute*                     /* dataset, schema */
Snapshot           ::= 'Snapshot' Identifier Attribute*                  /* source, version */
DataObject         ::= 'DataObject' Identifier Attribute*                /* may carry state */
DataInput          ::= '@in' NodeRef
DataOutput         ::= '@out' NodeRef

/* ========== Choreography ========== */
Choreography     ::= 'Choreography' Attribute* ParticipantRef+ InitiatingParticipant? MessageFlowList
ParticipantRef   ::= ProcessRef
InitiatingParticipant ::= ParticipantRef
MessageFlowList  ::= MessageFlow*
MessageFlow      ::= 'MessageFlow' Identifier Attribute* ParticipantRef '->' ParticipantRef

/* ========== Gateways ========== */
Gateway          ::= 'Gateway' Identifier GatewayAttribute*
GatewayAttribute ::= GatewayType | Attribute
GatewayType      ::= '@type' ('Random' | 'StratifiedAllocation' | 'Eligibility' |
                              'Exclusive' | 'Parallel' | 'Inclusive' | 'Complex')
SequenceFlow     ::= 'SequenceFlow' Identifier Attribute* NodeRef '->' NodeRef
                                                            /* optional conditionExpression */

/* ========== Common definitions ========== */
Attribute             ::= Identifier Value
ProcessRef            ::= Identifier
NodeRef               ::= Identifier

/* ========== Basic value types ========== */
Boolean    ::= 'true' | 'false'
Value      ::= String | Number | Boolean | Identifier
Number     ::= '-'? ( [0-9]+ ('.' [0-9]*)? | '.' [0-9]+ )
String     ::= '"' [^"]* '"'
Identifier ::= [A-Za-z] [A-Za-z0-9_]*
```


## 5.5 The runner interface

The runner is a separate client-side application that walks one diagram node by node for either a person or an artificial agent (§2.3), and its extensibility, its traversal, its validation, and its executor all rest on a small set of source structures. Figure 8 shows the executor design and §3.2 shows the runner administering the battery; this subsection gives the architecture behind them.

A node directory makes the runner extensible the same way the schema layer makes the modeler extensible. Each node kind the runner can execute is one subfolder under `src/runner/nodes/`, and adding a kind means adding one folder. Auto-discovery imports every `<kind>/index.tsx` at startup, and each one self-registers in a registry that rejects a duplicate type. The contract a folder implements is the `NodeDefinition` interface, which carries the three pieces §2.3 describes plus an optional validator: a matcher that recognizes which diagram elements the kind handles, a mapper (`toJob`) that extracts the runtime parameters from an element, a React component that renders the step, and a `validate` function for the kind's preconditions. The matcher resolves by a fixed precedence, trying the namespaced extension type first, then the BPMN type, and finally a `task` fallback, so a domain group can ship a custom step (an eye-tracking calibration or a VR scene) without forking the runner. The folders that ship today are the six built-in kinds of §2.3 (start, end, instruction, questionnaire, cognitive task, and a generic-task fallback).

Traversal is a single generator over the graph, and the phase the interface shows tracks where that generator is. The graph walk is the async generator `Session.traverse()` in `src/runner/session.ts`, which starts at the diagram's start node, yields one job per node, and stops when it reaches the end job. The runner reflects progress as a phase string in `Runner.tsx` that moves through `idle`, `loading`, `running`, and a per-step `job:<type>`, then settles on `done`, or on `error`, `invalid`, or `aborted`. Gateway semantics live in the same file: a random gateway and a stratified-allocation gateway both pick an outgoing branch uniformly through one `pickRandomBranch` helper, so stratified allocation currently falls back to uniform (§2.3); an exclusive or inclusive gateway evaluates conditions against a runtime variable store and otherwise takes a default branch; and a parallel gateway raises an explicit not-supported error, which marks it as a scope choice rather than a silent gap.

Validation runs in the three layers §2.3 names, and the runner enforces the last before it walks the graph: a per-step validator is the `validate` member of a node kind, returning issues keyed by node, and if any reports an issue the runner sets the phase to `invalid` rather than starting a partial run. The cognitive-battery validator, for example, checks each task against the assessment manifest and flags an unknown scene, an empty configuration, an unknown timeline, or a malformed bot specification.

The executor is the central architectural claim, and the runner realizes it as one message interface that many actor packages stand behind. The design draws on the actor model of concurrent computation, where addressable entities hold private state and act only on the messages they receive [@hewitt1973actor; @agha1986actors]. The runner defines a single executor with the signature `executor(stimulus, responses, timing, frame?) -> (response, response_time)` (Figure 8): per trial it marshals the stimulus, the allowed responses, the timing constraint, and, where a model needs it, a rendered frame into the actor, and it records the response and, where applicable, the response time under the common schema. Each actor keeps whatever private state its kind needs behind that interface, so the runner never reaches inside it; §3.2 walks the four actors this study fills. The language already types each actor by `actorType` (human, LLM, agent, or instrument; §2.1), and the `Actor` element carries the slots an external package needs to identify itself, including a model identifier, a prompt template, an agent specification such as a CogEnv profile or a checkpoint hash, and an instrument specification such as an LSL stream name.

Two of the four actor packages run as live code in this repository, and two are external packages reached through the same interface; §3.2 describes the four as actors. The human package and the language-model package are in the runner, the latter with provider backends for a local Ollama server and a commercial Claude model and with the rendered frame for vision-capable models, and both write to one trials table (BDM [@bdm], Psych-DS-compatible [@psychds]). The reinforcement-learning package CogEnv [@ansarinia2022cogenv] and the recurrent-model package CogPonder [@ansarinia2023cogponder] are external, reached through the same interface rather than living in the runner. The bot interface itself is the per-trial request and reply the runner exchanges with the Behaverse assessment application over a message bridge: the assessment runtime is mounted at `assessment-unity`, the runner receives an awaiting-response event carrying the trial index, the stimulus, the response options, the maximum response time, and an optional screenshot, and it injects the chosen response back. A reply may come from a built-in bot, a runner-side uniform-random choice, or a language-model call per trial, and the out-of-set fallback that keeps a transient failure from corrupting the dataset is the one stated in §2.3. The multi-turn and choreography exchanges remain a roadmap item (§4.5).

## 5.6 Reproducibility and availability

Reproducibility in Studyflow has a precise, deliberately limited scope: the seed fixes the protocol a co-subject encounters, and responses are recorded rather than fixed. When a seed is present in the URL, the runner seeds a `mulberry32` generator for branch selection, so the control flow, path allocation, and within-task stimulus order are identical across runs; the per-trial responses are sampled, so we record the seed with the model identity and version and report agent results as run-level aggregates rather than one canonical trace (§3.2). The seed is conventionally `42`. The runner also fingerprints the source XML with a SHA-256 hash and pins every telemetry event to it, so each recorded row ties to the exact source document that produced it.

The publication path is versioned on the server, so studies already in the field keep working as authors push updates. The publish action uploads a diagram to the Behaverse Data Server at `https://api.behaverse.org/v1` [@bds], which builds its own participant-facing interface from the diagram structure and ignores the local modeler layout (§2.2). Each publish creates a new server-side version, and earlier versions stay reachable by identifier, so an update does not break a running study. In the worked data examples, datasets bind to a backing store such as a DuckDB-plus-Parquet ducklake (§3.3); the ducklake appears in the example and the documentation as the chosen backing store rather than as a runtime requirement of the runner.

All artifacts are open source under the MIT license and run in the browser without installation. The Code and data availability section lists the hosting and source locations, the canonical schema repository, the example diagrams that ship with the modeler, and the steps to reproduce each figure and runner figure at seed 42.

# Code and data availability


All artifacts are open source under the MIT license and run in the browser without installation. The modeler, runner, and corresponding documentation are hosted at [behaverse.org/studyflow-modeler/app](https://behaverse.org/studyflow-modeler/app), and the source codes are available at [github.com/behaverse/studyflow-modeler](https://github.com/behaverse/studyflow-modeler). The canonical schema is versioned separately at [github.com/behaverse/schemas](github.com/behaverse/schemas). The versions used in this paper are tagged in the repository.

Example diagrams referenced in the paper ship with the modeler: a CONSORT 2025-style randomized trial, a SPIRIT 2025 schedule of enrolment and assessment, a base demo, and three agent-profiling demos (`bot_external.studyflow`, a randomized baseline; `bot_claude.studyflow`, a commercial language model; and `bot_ollama.studyflow`, a local open-weight model). Reproducing every figure requires opening the corresponding diagram in the hosted modeler and exporting SVG. Runner figures are reproduced by loading the same files into the runner with seed 42. Permanent links to the exact source commits will be added to the camera-ready version.

# Supplementary materials

## Table S1. The Studyflow element catalog

The catalog below lists the elements of the always-loaded layers (the language core and the companion cognitive layer). Every element specializes a standard BPMN type, given in the *BPMN base* column, so a diagram remains valid BPMN 2.0 and degrades gracefully in a generic BPMN tool. Four optional domain layers (a cognitive assessment battery, a generic process orchestration layer, a large-scale data transformation layer, and a multimodal acquisition layer for EEG and eye tracking) add further specialized elements that plug in without changing the core. The element types, their attributes, and validation rules are generated from the versioned LinkML schema, which is the authoritative source.
